summary:
In March 2025 the Athena lander came down on its side near the Moon's south pole. Its solar panels could not recharge it, and the mission ended about 13 hours after landing. On the Moon, sunlight and a view of Earth decide how long a lander can work. So if your landing slips nine days, what do you lose in the first 72 hours?

Long Shadow answers that on one screen. Pick a landing site, a touchdown date and a delay. It shows how many hours the Sun and Earth are above the horizon in each case, when each one rises or sets, and what the delay costs or gains. The Sun is the lander's power and Earth is its radio link, so those hours decide what a mission can do.

It works for any point on the Moon and any touchdown from 2024 through 2030. Every Sun and Earth position comes from NASA JPL Horizons, and our numbers match direct JPL queries within 0.006 degrees. The globe is the real Moon, built from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter maps.

The challenge asks for a tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare landing sites and dates quickly. Long Shadow does that in a browser, with no login, no install and no live data connection.
details:
The problem

Most landers run on sunlight and talk to Earth by direct radio. Blue Ghost stopped after sunset on March 16, 2025, and Chandrayaan-3 never woke after its first lunar night. Landing dates slip, and on the Moon a few days change everything. The Sun moves about 12 degrees across the lunar sky each Earth day. JPL Horizons gives exact numbers, but one query at a time, as text tables.

What Long Shadow does

- Any site, any touchdown from 2024 through 2030, any slip from 1 to 30 days. Nine real landing sites are built in, or type any latitude and longitude.

- Hours of Sun, Earth and both above the horizon, for the original and delayed dates, with each rise and set.

- Go or no go against a mission need, a strip of all 31 slips, a backup finder, a table of every site and a calendar of every date.

- A heatmap of the whole 3D Moon, real LOLA terrain skylines, a terrain margin and eclipses.

- Deep Space Network coverage from Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra, matched to JPL within 0.004 degrees.

- Stays of 72 hours, 7 days or a full lunar day of 709 hours, and a far-side relay view for Chang'e 4 and 6 (illustrative orbits).

- Timelines, a mission clock, a 3D globe and lander view, CSV download and share links.

What it found

At Athena's site, a March 15, 2025 touchdown has the Sun up all 72 hours and Earth up 66.5. Slip nine days and the Sun never rises, and Earth is up 17.8 hours. Against a 24 hour need, that turns a go into a no go. The earliest backup is a one day slip.

How we know it is right

200 Sun and Earth directions at 10 sites and 10 dates match direct JPL Horizons queries within 0.006 degrees. The model puts Blue Ghost's sunset at 20:11 UTC on March 16, 2025, and its eclipse window covers NASA's March 14, 2025 totality. 130 automated tests pass.

Tools

JavaScript, Vite, three.js, Vitest, Python. Static site on Vercel.

Code: https://github.com/Arnav66692/NASA-Space-Apps-Challenge-2026
dataRefs: NASA JPL Horizons System (Sun and Earth positions, 2024 to 2030)
